title: Self-report is a prior, not proof
statement: Treat what a student says they know as a starting guess that their answers can overturn, never as proof of mastery.
example: About 80% of students check a word as known, about 50% can give an example, and about 20% can explain it.
detail: A diagnostic BrainLift in the reading project's knowledge base counts self-report as a legitimate, underused signal for setting priors, under one design principle: self-report is a prior, not a verdict, so it shifts probabilities but doesn't override item evidence. The platform's rules say not to advance students on time, completion or self-report. For word knowledge the gap is wide: a finding cited in the reading BrainLift has about 80% of students checking a word as known, about 50% able to give an example and about 20% able to explain it.
against: The diagnostic evidence base says students judge coarse topic knowledge better than the assessment literature implies, though they are poor at predicting exact scores, so outside word knowledge self-report may be closer to the truth.
